topic: myths (unrealistic expectations set by admissions marketing) / mental health
speaker_role: faculty psychologist, not an admissions professional (Dr. Tim Bono, faculty advisor for WashU's Peer Counseling Center)
commercial_incentive: None - academic TEDx talk with no products or services promoted
key_insights: The talk's core admissions-adjacent point: college admissions presentations and campus tours tend to paint an idealized, uniformly positive picture of college life that can inflate prospective students' expectations

Survey data cited: 66% of college presidents named student mental health their top non-academic concern; in a separate survey, 66% of students reported overwhelming anxiety and 46% reported depression severe enough to impair functioning

Uses the formula 'happiness = what you have / what you want' to argue that unrealistic expectations set during the admissions/recruiting process (inflating the denominator) directly contribute to student disappointment and disillusionment once enrolled

Argues this isn't a criticism of admissions offices doing their job (generating excitement is appropriate) but a call for prospective students/families to seek out a fuller, more realistic picture beyond tours and marketing

Notes the happiest students aren't happy all the time - they have realistic expectations about inevitable hardships (roommate conflicts, disappointing classes, missed opportunities) and pre-existing coping strategies or know who to turn to for help
specific_numbers_or_facts: 66% of surveyed college presidents (Chronicle of Higher Education survey) named student mental health their top concern
66% of students reported overwhelming anxiety and 46% reported depression impairing function (American College Health Association data cited)
notable_or_distinctive: Offers a genuinely underdiscussed critique of the admissions marketing/tour process itself as a contributing cause of post-enrollment mental health struggles, rather than addressing the admissions decision process directly - as the batch note flags, this is only tangentially about admissions.
reliability_notes: This is a general mental-health/psychology talk, not admissions guidance; it contains no advice about applications, essays, or decisions, and its relevance here is limited to one observation about how campus marketing shapes expectations. Cited statistics are attributed to named surveys but exact methodology/dates are not given in the transcript.
